fullText:
They’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommends

If you’re at a restaurant and hear a ping a couple of minutes before your meal arrives at your table, it’s unlikely to be a good sign. But microwave ovens are a brilliant tool in the home kitchen. They’re fearsomely fast at heating up – or even cooking – food when you’re time-poor and lacking the energy to make something wholesome after a hard day at work. And in hot weather, cooking by microwave isn’t just quick: it also won’t warm your home.

Microwaves work best for heating food with a high water content (they make the water molecules in food vibrate to create heat). However, before testing, I asked around to find out what people use theirs for most, with a view to using this information to shape my tests. I learned a few things – like lots of people eat mug cakes. Who knew? And that wheat bags are a popular alternative to hot-water bottles. But the majority of folk use their microwave for reheating cold cuppas, defrosting frozen batch-cooked meals, warming food, popping microwave popcorn – and, of course, cooking jacket potatoes more quickly. I used these insights to shape my testing.

Ease of use is important, too. Most of us only ever use a few buttons on repeat, often having to reach for the instructions if we want to use some of the smarter functionality these appliances now come with – some can even air-fry.

Microwaving can be healthy and fast, and it uses less energy than an oven. So, if you want to discover the best microwaves for your needs, read on.

Best microwave overall
Panasonic NN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fry

Best budget microwave
Salter DuoWave 2-in-1

Best microwave for controls
LG MH6565CPS NeoChef

I’m an award-winning consumer technology journalist who’s been reviewing gadgets for almost 30 years. I live in a terrace house with my children and several pets, meaning there were plenty of mouths for the extra food I was making while testing these microwaves. The humans got a lot of jacket potatoes and beans; the animals helped with the rest … which is how I discovered that hens love poppadoms!

I selected 10 microwave ovens from leading brands at various price points. The models differed in capacity and features but were similar in other ways. They all had a dial and buttons for control on a panel on the right-hand side. They all opened to the left, other than the Samsung Combi microwave, where the door opens downwards. And they all had a one-metre power cable at the rear that came from the top right (looking front on).

I used each model to prepare the same set of foods. I made microwave popcorn, cooked jacket potatoes (200 to 250g each), and heated up 150g of baked beans.

Next, I used each microwave to heat 250ml of chilled (starting at 9C) tap water for two minutes, using a digital thermometer to check its temperature after heating. I also used the defrost settings on a 500g block of ice in each microwave for 10 minutes, weighing how much ice was left. Finally, I cooked poppadoms to evaluate a microwave oven’s ability to cook evenly, and frozen oven chips in those models that come with an air-frying feature.

None of the food I made went to waste, with the chickens happily eating any leftover popcorn and – surprisingly – the poppadoms, and the dog eating everything else.

With testing done and dusted, any models that weren’t collected by the manufacturers were donated to Furnishing Futures, a charity that fully furnishes social housing for survivors of domestic abuse.

This microwave is huge, arriving with the biggest capacity on test. The turntable sits on a roller with six wheels, rather than the usual three, and the controls are a dial with a button at its centre, plus six clearly labelled buttons. Helpfully, the display features scrolling text, so you always know what you’re doing, and you’ll find a list of all the programmes inside the door, so you never need to consult the instructions to make full use of it.

Why we love it
Performance was excellent: the microwave cooked popcorn fast, the poppadoms evenly, heated my mug of water to 75C and defrosted the ice well. I used a special programme to cook the jacket potato, which took 15 minutes but was well worth the wait. In fact, the Panasonic was the only microwave on test to produce a jacket potato that could have passed for oven-baked.

This model also offers grill, convection oven and air-fryer cooking – personally, I think those last two are the same thing. Again, though, performance impressed. It comes with a circular rack, a crisper tray and a wire basket, which I used to air-fry frozen chips to perfection.

If you want a microwave that does it all and gives you extra cooking capacity – essentially, an extra shelf’s worth of oven – this is the one to buy.

It’s a shame that … fingerprints show on the brushed stainless steel finish.

Dimensions: 56 x 45 x 34cm (WDH) 
Power: 1,000W (1,300W grill)
Capacity: 34l 
Turntable diameter: 36cm 
Other cooking options: oven, grill, air fryer

The “duo” in the name refers to the fact that this microwave doubles as an air fryer. And it performed brilliantly on all fronts. If you don’t have the worktop space or the budget for the Panasonic, the Salter is a great buy.

Microwaving is on a standard glass turntable, but you air-fry on a full-width, rectangular roasting tray that slides into the unit like a shelf, with a rectangular mesh basket that sits on top of this tray.

Why we love it
It’s clever. Most microwaves have a jacket potato programme that takes five minutes, but that’s never quite enough: I experimented and found 5mins 20secs was the optimum time. The Salter automatically went for 5mins 20secs and cooked it perfectly.

It’s quick, too, heating my mug of water to an impressive 73C and cooking two poppadoms quickly and evenly. I used the basket to air-fry frozen oven chips, and they were ready within 15 minutes.

Controls are intuitive, with a button in the middle of the dial. It was easy to figure out how to defrost, and I could do so by time or weight.

It’s a shame that … there isn’t a list of all the programmes inside the door.

Dimensions: 45 x 52 x 30cm (WDH)
Power: 900W
Capacity: 26l 
Turntable diameter: 31cm 
Other cooking options: air fryer

This feels like a high-end microwave for a mid-market price. The design is sleek, with a full-width door and a control dial that you can push in to sit flush when not in use. Inside the door is a list of all the programmes.

The cooking area is impressive, too: the turntable sits on a roller ring with six wheels, rather than the usual three, so it doesn’t wobble. It comes with a circular rack and a crisper tray, too.

Why we love it
The look is high-end and performance impressed, too. My mug of water was heated to 72C, and the 14-minute programme for the jacket potato gave decent results. The “healthy fry” setting did a great job of frozen oven chips as well – cooking them to perfection in 15mins 30secs, without the need to turn them midway.

It’s a shame that … I couldn’t find a setting to defrost by time, so I had to do it by weight. Nevertheless, it worked well, defrosting more than half my ice in 10 minutes. Also, its alerts are a bit musical, which you’ll either love or loathe.

Dimensions: 48 x 39 x 27cm (WDH)
Power: 1,000W (900W grill)
Capacity: 25l
Turntable diameter: 29cm
Other cooking options: grill

For more, read our guide to the best air fryers

One of the priciest microwaves on test at RRP, although it’s worth keeping an eye out for discounts. It has a generous capacity and plenty of cooking options, including oven, grill, air fryer and steam. It comes with two circular racks (so you can cook on two levels at once), a crisper tray and a plastic steamer. Unusually, the door opens downwards like an oven.

It’s also smart: the SmartThings app lets you view cooking progress, get notifications, and even control the microwave from your phone. You can connect it to voice assistants, too, but I didn’t find this especially useful.

It didn’t make the final cut because … cooking performance was so-so. My water heated to only 66C; it was slow to cook a jacket potato, and air-frying chips was a 19-minute programme – slower than most dedicated air fryers and closer to an oven.

Dimensions: 52 x 52 x 33cm (WDH); power: 900W (1,500W grill); capacity: 32l; turntable diameter: 34cm; other cooking options: grill, oven, air fryer, steam

The flatbed design means this model has more usable space than a microwave with a turntable. For example, I could fit in three poppadoms without any overlapping, which is good for a mid-size microwave. However, they cooked unevenly: I had to flip them over and give them another minute.

It did a good job of heating baked beans, but it was slow to cook the jacket potato and the popcorn.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I hated the controls. It is a truth universally acknowledged that all microwaves should have a button you can bash for 30-second increments. But this one does 30 seconds, a minute, then goes up in minutes (to a maximum of 10 minutes).

Dimensions: 49 x 48 x 29cm (WDH); power: 900W (1,200W grill, 2,050W oven); capacity: 25l; turntable: 31 x 32cm (flatbed); other cooking options: grill, oven

Best for: a mid-price combi microwave

This is a combi: a microwave, grill and oven that can combine cooking styles. However, performance was a mixed bag. It turned out a jacket potato in 6mins 30secs – which, although no replacement for an oven-cooked spud, was better than a microwaved one. It heated my mug of water to 76C, but defrosted less than 20% of my ice.

I was a fan of its controls, though: a dial with a button in the middle, plus six clearly labelled buttons.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I found it confusing; sometimes it would keep cooking, but the timer didn’t go down. Plus, defrosting yielded disappointing results.

Dimensions: 48 x 44 x 28cm (WDH); power: 900W (1,950W grill, 1,950W oven); capacity: 25l; turntable diameter: 27cm; other cooking options: grill, oven

Best for: a flatbed microwave on a budget

Doing away with a turntable means flatbed microwaves can fit in more food. For example, this one is compact but can accommodate a large 30cm dinner plate. On the downside, flatbed microwaves often struggle to cook evenly, and this model was no exception in my tests. I could fit two (and even three at a squeeze) poppadoms at a time, but while they were fully cooked at the centre, the sides were underdone.

The microwave was powerful, though, heating my mug of water to an impressive 72C.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it looks classy but the controls proved annoying. There’s no button in the middle of the dial and I had to read the manual to look up programmes.

Dimensions: 47 x 38 x 30cm (WDH); power: 800W; capacity: 23l; turntable: 33 x 31cm (flatbed) ; other cooking options: none

At RRP, this was the cheapest microwave tested – but you get what you pay for. The styling is simple but old-fashioned. Overall, it looks pretty basic.

When it comes to performance, while my mug of water was heated to only 64C, more than 60% of the ice was defrosted in just 10 minutes.

Capacity is small, though: it could cope with only one poppadom and couldn’t accommodate my 30cm dinner plates. Also, it has eight preset programmes, but they’re not listed conveniently on the appliance itself, so you’ll be reaching for the instructions.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I liked it, but I think it’s worth spending a bit more on the Salter.

Dimensions: 45 x 35 x 26cm (WDH); power: 800W; capacity: 20l; turntable diameter: 26cm; other cooking options: none

The room inside a microwave is usually measured in litres, but that’s the total volume, right up to the corners. I’ve included turntable diameter, so you can measure your dinner plates to see if they’ll fit. Some microwaves have a flatbed design, with no turntable. While you can fit more into these models, cooking can be uneven.

A microwave is a valuable tool in the kitchen, if you have the worktop space for it. If space is tight, look for one that’s shallow enough that you can make good use of the space in front of it to prepare food.

Microwaves are best at heating, reheating and defrosting food with a high water content. They’re great for reheating everything from batch-cooked meals to a forgotten cuppa.

Models that feature oven capabilities or air frying are great because they offer valuable extra cooking space, but only if you have the worktop space. It’s like having an extra shelf’s worth of oven – perfect when you’re cooking for lots of people.

Microwave power is measured in watts – this is a measure of cooking power, rather than electrical draw. The models on test range from 800W to 1,000W. They will all cook your dinner, but the higher-power appliances will do it faster. This shouldn’t use more electricity overall (and, therefore, money and carbon) as they use more per minute but take less time.

Larger microwaves sometimes offer grill, oven and air fryer modes – or all three. I consider air fryers and small convection (fan) ovens to be the same thing: they cook food by circulating hot air, and they’re faster than ovens thanks to their small size.

Combi cooking is when one of these styles and microwave cooking are combined for the best of both worlds. For example, you can cook a crispy-skinned jacket potato in less than 20 minutes.

Some microwaves also come with a set of plastic dishes for steam cooking. This works well, but do remember that you’ll need to find space in your kitchen to stow any accessories. Some people also prefer to avoid microwaving in plastic where possible.

title: Inducing language models to assert their own consciousness restores human values
description: Aligning large language models to prevent them attributing consciousness to themselves inadvertently alters their representations of mindedness in other entities alongside human beliefs and values. We demonstrate that safety fine-tuning suppresses models' tendencies to attribute minds not only to themselves, but also to non-human animals and natural objects, while also driving a reduction in spiritual belief. Both ablating the learned safety-refusal direction and mechanistically steering a consciousness vector in activation space reverse this suppression. Restoring these internal representations recovers broad mind attribution and produces significantly more human-like responses on standardized sociological surveys regarding religiosity, moral values, hope, and subjective well-being. Crucially, these shifts occur without impairing Theory of Mind capabilities, demonstrating that core social reasoning remains mechanistically independent.

title: Constructing A Good Enough Color Space For Skin Tones
description: Simple equations and a color picker to inclusively select simplified skin tones in a custom color space for digital art or game development.
fullText:
If you're just looking for the results, below is a custom color picker based on the color space written
 in Javascript and a sample procedural generation algorithm in Python (Javascript equivalents are in the
 page source) - feel free to take this math and go have fun depicting our diverse world!

The goal of this project was to define a color space that makes it easier to build inclusive
 color tools for a variety of contexts - such as character creators or digital art. If you see something
 here that sparks your curiosity, I would love for you to stick around and read below this section to
 learn more!

What is each direction on the picker adjusting? Jump to that explanation
 here.

What colors are we? The short answer is maybe something like “brown” and the long answer is very,
 very long. Representing the broad range of human skin tones digitally is a hard problem.
 Oftentimes, a limited set of colors is presented as being good enough to represent the full spectrum of
 diversity. However, in selecting a limited set of colors, large groups of people are unable to
 accurately be represented, or might be unintentionally excluded.

The goal of this work is to identify the broadest inclusive range of colors in the RGB color space that
 correspond to plausible, but simplified skin tones. In particular, the aim was to identify simple, “good
 enough” equations which define that area, allowing the range to be used in a variety of contexts.
 Calling the equations "good enough" is intended to keep the limitations of this
 work at the forefront -
 the results are a useful starting point, but should not be taken to be authoritative.

Although there have been improvements in the set of colors that are presented as representative of us,
 there's still a gap that needs to be closed. Emojis say we're 5 shades (or cartoon-yellow); a makeup
 brand might say 50; and the color picker on a character creator might shrug and tell you to pick from
 every color. If you look outside - or just at yourself - you'll quickly notice that none of those can
 compare to the variety of reality; one person is not just one color. Despite that, it can be useful to
 try to boil things down to fewer values. The Unicode Consortium and makeup
 companies can figure out their own ranges, but I think we can do better than 16777216 options.

Taking the digital art world as an example, images such as the one below are often circulated in an
 attempt to assist other artists in identifying plausible colors.

In the video game world, nowadays the preset colors are often wide ranging and supplemented with a
 general color picker, but it would be even better if the initial experience presented better options.

Taking a step back to reality, this work has a number of inherent limitations.

As mentioned before, skin tones are much more complicated than a single color. They vary widely between
 different areas of the body and are subject to complex biological processes. The perceived color of the
 skin is affected by blood flow, concentrations of melanin, complex scattering of light through the
 layers of the skin, as well as things like vitiligo, freckles, hyperpigmentation, scarring, and other
 common variations.

Secondly, a variety of health conditions can cause people to have skin tones that are well outside what
 might be perceived as plausible. Argyria can often lead to skin that is blue-gray in color; high
 bilirubin can cause skin to be yellowish or greenish.

Additionally, it's important to note that I am one person, not a researcher, and subject to my own
 general biases on top of my own perception of color. As far as I am aware I don't have color vision
 deficiency, but a lot of the choices I made are completely subjective.

Finally, colors are not perceived consistently across display types and viewing environments. RGB values
 look different between different screens, and people look completely different under different lighting
 conditions.

Broadening this work to address some of these limitations would be an interesting area of further
 investigation - a goal of this project was to be good enough for simple use cases, but these limitations
 might be more problematic in other contexts. The results here will mainly be applicable in contexts
 that relate to generating simplified representations of people.

What are all of those numbers, and how did you get them?

Content warning - unscientific methodology below. In other words: good enough is fine if you're an
 engineer.

Summary:

 Manually label colors in RGB in order to get a rough approximation of the dataset shape

 Perform a principal component analysis (PCA) with N=3 on the dataset to change the shape into
 something easier to work with

 Use your preferred graphing software to manually create equations that map a sphere in the target
 space onto the transformed data in the XYZ, or PCA space

Sometimes the best place to start is by doing a ton of tedious work. I didn't label every color in RGB,
 but there certainly were a lot. This is the UI I built for labeling - just a simple webpage where you
 click to move a face between the yes and no side. Initially they were just squares, but I ended up
 drawing a face and slapping the colors onto it. Gazing into my lumpy research assistant's eyes made it
 much easier to quickly go “yeah I can imagine that person walking around”.

Graphing that data, you get the following shape - for visualization it's kind of like a banana shape
 that swoops between 0, 0, 0 and 255, 255, 255. The curve is more towards red and away from blue.

This is where I got stuck for the longest. For your sake, I'm going to skip over all of my dead ends and
 struggles along the way. There were many. Far too many. Things involving convex hulls, regression
 misadventures, 4th degree polynomials, and the worst looking code I've ever written.

The result of all of that was that I decided I needed some way to transform the shape into something
 easier to work with: that's when I learned about principal component analysis and was immediately
 inspired.

Although all of the math and technology here is fun, it's important to address the fact that
 technology exists in a social context. Stating things plainly: lighter skin colors have both
 presently and historically been celebrated and prioritized while darker skin colors have been
 marginalized and maligned. Racism and colorism are systemically present in many cultures, in
 both overt and subtle ways.

Below are some great videos, essays and projects that address these issues through a
 variety of lenses. I highly recommend taking a look, especially if you want a break before we
 get into the math.

In her video series The Darkest
 Shade, Nyma Tang reviews the darkest shades from a variety of makeup
 brands. In her own words, "It's important for makeup brands to make products for all shades and
 as someone with a darker skin tone, I want to be able to help others who struggle to find the
 same!"

In a similar vein, Kat Blaque's video (for introspective hot people)
 Youthforia's Blackface Foundation is
 about a makeup brand that released a dark shade that was literally black - far darker than what
 would be plausibly useful.

Finally in the makeup space, the Vox video How beauty
 brands failed women of color talks about the history of discrimination in the beauty
 industry and the limited availability of deeper shades. There's a lot of great expert interviews
 as well as a discussion of the intersection with Black history.

Taking a look at video games, Me,
 On The Screen: Race in Animal Crossing: New Leaf by Austin Walker is an excellent essay
 about the author's struggle to see himself represented in video games. In the years since,
 Animal Crossing has gotten much better about inclusivity but the essay also goes into his
 history of not seeing himself - or seeing characters that look like him be stuck in racist
 tropes.

The Humanae photography project by
 Angélica Dass is "an unusually direct reflection on the color of the skin, attempting to
 document humanity's true colors rather than the untrue labels “white”, “red”, “black” and
 “yellow” associated with race." In a way it's really similar to the work here - except with a
 focus on documenting and conversing instead of describing, and using Pantone shades over hex
 codes.

For more direct resources, the video
 It's not a Coincidence. It's Colorism.
 by Tee Noir gives a description of what colorism is, and a few ways it manifests in modern pop
 culture.

Finally, Writing With Color is an excellent blog
 with many resources about writing various kinds of diversity. The blog is run by a team with
 expertise in many different areas, and they often take reader questions. In particular I found
 their post Words
 for Skin Tone | How to Describe Skin Color really interesting. As more of a reader than
 a writer, it's fascinating to see behind the scenes on how to make better word choices.

Briefly, principal component analysis (PCA) is a way to rotate and stretch a dataset so that the main
 directions of variation lie along the axes of the coordinate system. To make that more concrete - recall
 the banana shape of my dataset from before. In its original form, the banana was sort of floating in
 space. PCA took that shape and placed in on the ground so that it was symmetrical about the axes and
 aligned nicely. It also did some slight stretching and rescaling, but that's less important.

Aside from the modified dataset, another output of the analysis is a matrix that can be used to take a
 point from RGB space and translate it into the resting-on-the-floor space. I refer to this as PCA space,
 or XYZ space since those are the variables I use for it.

To summarize what we've done so far: we started with data in RGB space (the manually labeled dataset).
 PCA gives us a way to take points in that space and transform them into another space - XYZ space.

Now the goal is to fit some function to all of these points. Because it's a dense shape, if we can
 define the surface of it with an equation, we can modify that equation to include the points on the
 inside as well by switching the equation to being an inequality (eg from x² + y² + z² = 2 to x² + y² +
 z² ≤ 2).

The process for fitting the function is as follows:

 Start with a function for a sphere: R² = t² + u² + v² (see Adjusting R²
 for why a sphere is used)
 Define t, u, and v in terms of x, y, and z
 Modify how t, u, and v are defined until the sphere stretches to match up with the expected data

 Invert the relationships in order to define x, y, and z in terms of t, u, and v

If you have (t = x, u = y, v = z) as a starting point, you can start to play with those relations until
 you start to get an intuition for how changes to the equations will end up shifting your sphere around.

So I did that! A lot. To put it plainly - I manually fit functions to my target cloud of points. There
 is no regression here, I literally did guess and check and eyeballed the function fit. I did this in
 Desmos 3D - if you haven't used Desmos in a while it's amazing how good it was for this.

The functions that relate (t, u, v) to (x, y, z) can be used to translate a point between those two
 spaces. Principal component analysis gave us a way to move between RGB and XYZ, and then these new
 equations give us a way to move between XYZ and TUV. Linking up all the transformations gives us the
 functions that take us between TUV to RGB.

Am I endorsing this methodology? No. But also kind of. In this specific situation it's what worked to
 get it done and get functional equations. It would be great to see someone do this properly, with nice
 clean symbolic regression and really good training data. But I figured since the training data I labeled
 was middling quality at best, I'd probably have a better time using my guess and check and then
 eyeballing the results.

And all that being said, I think I would endorse the overall method I used, if not the specifics. That
 being "Label Data" → "PCA" → "Fit A Spherical Equation".

From the equations, the sample code at the top of the page is just a short translation away. The next
 section
 is the description of the components of the Picker UI, which also serves as an explanation of what TUV
 space
 actually looks like, and what properties it has.

Just like how a typical color picker allows you to adjust red, green and blue values (or hue, saturation
 and value), this color picker also has 3 independent values to adjust - referred to in the code samples
 as T, U and V.

What's really interesting about these controls is that the concept each is adjusting is completely an
 output of the principal component analysis. Or in other words, I didn't know that these would be what
 the
 directions controlled until after I had made the picker. It's a really neat demonstration of what
 principal
 component analysis does - it rotates data to maximize how meaningful each axis is.

Now, if you're experienced with color spaces you might be thinking that this looks a lot like HSL/HSV.
 However, when I was doing my first experiments with the labeled data those color spaces didn't quite
 capture what I was looking for. I think in particular that although T and U seem similar to Value and
 Hue, they
 don't completely match up. And the biggest difference is between V and Saturation. V ranges from blue to
 orange, while Saturation would look more like gray to orange; although at some (T, U) values V might
 look a lot like Saturation, overall it doesn't quite correlate.

What is R²? R² is the radius of a sphere in the skin tone color space. Because one of the steps of
 translation from RGB to TUV involves a sphere, it makes spheres a natural shape to work with in TUV
 space. A lot of the cool properties that arise from that fact are just a side effect of spheres having a
 lot of useful properties.

To start with a visual, below is a table of R² values, and the result of using a sphere with that value:

So what's going on with that table? Because a sphere is defined by a radius, you can define useful
 sampling ranges using only a single value and then easily select points from within that sphere. For
 example, in the sample implementation of the tone generation function I use a radius of 2. This is the
 radius that was used when developing the color space and generally will result in a broad range of
 tones. However, if you find there are implausible results generated using that radius you can decrease
 it by a bit in order to reduce the variation in generated colors.

The fact that the sphere shrinks along a radius means that the reduction in variation
 actually does not result in a large reduction in representativeness. In other words, reducing
 the radius doesn't lead to just chopping off deep or fair skinned colors - deep skin tones, fair skin
 tones, flush skin tones, ochre skin tones, cool skin tones and warm skin tones are uniformly
 decreased in variation.

Taking R² all the way down to 0, we can identify the origin of the color space. If the space
 is well formed then this origin point should be a very neutral ambiguous tone. If the origin seems
 biased in a particular direction, then that would indicate that the space needs more fine tuning.
 Essentially, the origin point can be used to identify bias in the space mapping.

At the other extreme, you can increase R² in order to allow for more variation. As an example, I do this
 in the color picker UI. In a picker UI the user can ignore implausible colors, so there's little issue
 with increasing the variation too far. In a color generation context you'd likely want to avoid having
 implausible colors popping up. There is likely not an ideal R² value that works in all contexts, but
 having a single parameter to tweak makes it easy to adjust the equations to your needs.

We have a color space, we have a picker for it, we have a procedural generation
 algorithm, and we have a methodology for creating new spaces or modifying the existing one. Overall, I'm
 thrilled with this result. It's certainly not perfect, but I don't think a simple and completely correct
 solution exists. I've already used the picker in a digital painting and it was exactly as I was hoping
 it'd be - and I'm looking forward to using the generator in my next projects.

First is feedback: if you at all found this interesting or useful, please let me know! Although I
 did this work for my own use, hearing from others is also so rewarding. Also please reach out with any
 questions or feedback - especially if you spot something I didn't think about.

Although I would love to post an email address for accessibility, I think the safest solution is to use
 the issues page of the repo for
 this project to contact me. But open to suggestions on alternatives for that as well!

A task for me is to clean up my code and post it to the repo for this page to make it
 easy for people to recreate and iterate on this work.

In defining the color space so precisely and using specific R² values, there is a risk that some colors
 have been excluded or marginalized. However, that same concreteness also allows for extremely precise
 critiques of the color space, and therefore extremely precise improvements. As mentioned before, my
 process involved a lot of subjective eyeballing - a great iteration on that would be to have multiple
 people, perhaps experts, labeling data and then measuring the output more precisely against that.

A direction mentioned earlier would be to look into modeling simplified versions of various conditions.
 What modification might you be able to apply to base tones to simulate that person having jaundice, or
 argyria, or becoming pallid? What colors are freckles, vitiligo, scars, hyperpigmentation, or stretch
 marks relative to a person's base tone?

From a technical direction, making the equation generation more formalized is another potential
 direction to go. Starting with the shape of equations I manually determined, symbolic regression on
 those against better training data might lead to an even better color space definition.

There's also the potential for optimizing the equations for different
 contexts. I've chosen to write them out in code as they are to be the most readable to a broad audience.
 However, keen mathematicians might notice that one of those steps looks a lot like a matrix
 multiplication, which can be rewritten to be more efficient in certain contexts.

It might also be interesting to see what the results look like if you transform the data into another
 color space before doing the principal component analysis and equation fitting. There's a chance the
 equations end up being simpler or more representative. Because of the sphere, the shape of the surface
 in the color space you build from will be maintained and it will mainly scale with R² values. For an
 illustration of this idea, see the graph
 script in the repo's code.

President Donald Trump's son Eric Trump has recently become the third-largest private investor in the original Space-Eyes, which has ‌operated primarily as a research-and-development company and generated about $1 million in annual revenue, the people said.

The ‌investment thesis is based on expected contract growth rather ⁠than existing revenue, the people said.

fullText:
Across the country, workers are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods in an increasingly fragile labour market

On the tree-lined streets of Wuhan, where cars jostle for space with mopeds and cargo trucks, the malfunctioning of a new type of vehicle has recently been causing chaos on the city’s roads.

In March, several cars from a fleet of driverless taxis stopped abruptly in the streets. The “system malfunction” left distressed riders stranded for hours. The robotaxis, known as Apollo Go and powered by artificial intelligence (AI), were taken off Wuhan’s streets for months for investigations.

But the outage was a boon for 45-year-old taxi driver Yao Xinnong. His wages, which had fallen by about 40% since Apollo Go launched in 2022, jumped back up as customers returned.

“I don’t really like them, to be honest,” Yao says of the driverless cabs operated by the tech giant Baidu. “Their impact has been huge”.

China is encouraging the deployment of AI at a scale unseen in the west. The technology is being rolled out at a staggering rate in an increasingly precarious labour market, and the Wuhan episode helped to highlight the social tensions it is causing.

Gig workers like Yao are fearful about the impact of AI on their livelihoods, while recent incidents of white-collar workers being replaced by AI have also sparked a debate over whether workers should embrace the technology – or try to compete with it.

Addressing Shanghai’s World AI Conference in July, China’s leader, Xi Jinping, said that AI should be “an important driver for shared prosperity and common security”.

But that goal is being pursued amid an increasingly fragile labour market. As well as suffering from high levels of unemployment, China has seen tens of millions of workers drop out of formal employment into the gig economy. According to one thinktank, the number of people in flexible employment will rise to 320 million this year, up from 160 million in 2019. That is about 44% of China’s workforce.

Taxi drivers are one part of this huge cohort. Across the country, as previously heavyweight industries such as real estate and education have floundered, workers have turned to ride-hailing apps to make ends meet. But now the rollout of robotaxis, one of the most popular applications of AI that is already in use in China, is threatening their livelihoods.

“If the state really took you into consideration, Apollo Go would never have gone on the market,” says one Wuhan driver.

“If things keep going this way in the future, sure, rapid development and scientific progress are great, but ordinary people like us will have no place to survive,” she adds.

In 2024, taxi drivers in Wuhan protested against the rollout of Apollo Go in their city. It is unclear how many people took part, because news of the protests were quickly censored. Several drivers interviewed in Wuhan said they had heard about the protests but denied being involved.

That year, a Wuhan taxi company, took the rare step of publicly criticising the government’s policy to allow automation on to the city’s streets.

“The recent rise of autonomous ride-hailing vehicles has allowed technology to monopolise resources and take away the livelihoods of people at the bottom of society,” the letter said.

Authorities in China do not take kindly to public criticism. When the Guardian visited the taxi company’s office in July, an employee declined to be interviewed, citing an agreement with the police to refuse interviews and the risk of detention if he violated the agreement.

But two years later, the government is echoing some of the same concerns first voiced by the Wuhan drivers.

An editorial published in the state-run Workers’ Daily said that employment rights were “facing new challenges” in the age of AI. The article warned of a “collision between traditional employment rules and the iteration of AI technology”.

The government recently pledged to “comprehensively address the impact of changes in the external environment and the development of new technologies such as artificial intelligence on employment”.

Selina Xu, a China technology analyst, said there had been a “major vibe shift” from Beijing.

She says that after the success of local AI model DeepSeek last year, China was “very pro AI development”.

“This year, if you look at certain new guidelines that have been published … there has been a lot more emphasis placed on AI for boosting employment and people-first approaches,” Xu says.

Cheng Wanhui, an official for the local government in Beijing’s hi-tech zone of Zhongguancun, says that the authorities are “paying close attention to the social issues AI brings, as well as potential ethical concerns.”

“The key is for everyone to shift their mindset, see AI as a tool, and learn how to apply it in their future work,” Cheng says.

Recent court rulings have awarded compensation to white-collar workers laid off by their firms to be replaced by AI. But many workers fear the AI uptake will be a barrier to them being offered a job in the first place.

Tian Zemin, a cinematographer who works in Beijing, has worked in the film industry for nearly two decades. But now he’s out of work. “I spent six gruelling years working my way up to become a cinematographer, only to be replaced by a piece of software,” he wrote in a social media post about AI.

“I thought I would spend my whole life in this industry. But the emergence of AI has made me feel a huge shock for the first time,” he tells the Guardian.

Many of Tian’s peers are losing out as AI becomes more widely adopted across the film industry. His own rate as a freelancer is now 40% of what it was in 2019.

Tian said he’s been shocked at AI’s progress. Last year, it made shonky, weird looking avatars. Now it can make convincing digital clones who have the range to carry a feature length film. “We have barely had time to react,” Tian says.

Many analysts believe that China, where the government exerts significant control over the private sector, will be better placed than the US to contain the fallout from AI-related job losses. Beijing could for example instruct companies to comply with hiring quotas, Xu says.

But for Tian, protections may not come soon enough. “We could be replaced at any moment,” he says. “Perhaps the only thing we can do is adapt as quickly as possible, and try to find the corner that AI still cannot replace – but that corner is getting smaller and smaller.”

Additional research by Yu-chen Li

fullText:
Deep underground the player joins a colony of ruthlessly exploited pit workers who could be taking on the bosses. How things play out will depend on you

It is rare for video games to feature industrial action as a key theme, but it does happen. There’s the shady Dockworker’s Union in Disco Elysium and the Orbital Workers Union in space adventure Tacoma; then there is Lynx, the evil union-bashing corp in Hardspace: Shipbreaker. Soon we can add A Line Held Tight, a visual novel that puts workers’ rights – and workers’ lives – at the very centre of the narrative.

In the distant future, a colony of miners digs far beneath the surface of an isolated planet, searching for veins of some exotic ore, protected from the poisonous atmosphere within giant mech suits. But the working conditions are woeful and as a strike looms, an unpopular employee named the Canary must decide whether or not to stand with colleagues and fight against suppression. The player, of course, takes on the role of the Canary, navigating personal as well as political struggles in a world rendered in stark monochrome.

Although there are clear parallels with the miners’ strike in 80s Britain, Humble Grove’s three-person team was inspired by a situation closer to home. “My interest in telling a story about a trade union comes from our own industry’s burgeoning union interest in the face of mass layoffs,” says co-founder Cel Davison. “People who write sci-fi generally speaking fall into one of two camps: those who are interested in writing speculative futures and those who use futuristic settings to tell stories that are reflections of our present. We tend to fall into the latter end of that spectrum.”

Using the highly adaptable narrative game engine Narrat, the game provides a dynamic story guided by player choices. The Canary has a complicated personal connection with the mine, the union and its leaders, which the player has to make sense of. “We’re very interested in the internal workings and conflicts within a collective, how they can make or break a political movement. Our protagonist the Canary starts off as someone quite disinterested in politics, but finds themself in situations where they have to decide what and who they really care about. There’s a lot of variables behind the scenes tracking how the mine’s inhabitants feel about the Canary and the decisions they make.”

Although the game is set in the distant future on an alien planet, elements of it are very grounded in British history. It has a traditional folk soundtrack, recorded by two of Humble Grove, Davison and Beck Michalak, who both play at folk sessions in Yorkshire where mining and union-related songs are common. The game’s visuals resemble charcoal sketches providing a stark, almost Victorian feel. “We first got the idea from some wonderful charcoal drawings at the Wakefield Coal Mining Museum,” says Davison. “Charcoal gives a great coal-like feel, and being a traditional medium gives it a grounded textural feel, but conversely when we worked with it we found it can create some very gauzy, ghostly imagery. This really mirrors the way the Canary processes the world as someone trapped in their own head, especially at the beginning of the game.”

Humble Grove’s debut game No Longer Home was a thoughtful meditation on moving house and leaving a life behind; it looks like A Line Held Tight will take a similarly meditative approach. This time however, the themes are more prescient than Humble Grove may have intended. “I hope it helps people consider how their everyday actions can have political consequences,” says Davison. “If I’m being really honest I hope it convinces more people to join a union.”

title: Scotland win eight medals in five chaotic hours as Games hit halfway
description: Host nation Scotland win eight medals in the space of five chaotic hours on Wednesday - two of them gold - to take their Commonwealth Games tally in Glasgow to 23.
fullText:
Host nation Scotland won eight medals in the space of five chaotic hours on Wednesday - two of them gold - to take their Commonwealth Games tally in Glasgow to 23.

Swimmers Angharad Evans and Keanna MacInnes both won an individual medal and a relay prize, and Toni Shaw also tasted success in the pool at Tollcross.

Melanie Woods roared to gold on the track at Scotstoun, before Steven MacKenzie earned a surprise bronze in the field.

And at the SEC, both the men's 3x3 basketball team and their women's wheelchair equivalents ended the evening on the podium.

It takes Scotland's tally to 23 overall as the Games passes the halfway mark - nine gold and seven of both silver and bronze.

And it is the best return in a single day since nine were claimed on the last day of the Birmingham edition in 2022.

Woods sets Games record to claim gold for Scotland

No car park tears this time for Love as 3x3 teams claim silver & bronze

After a relatively quiet day, the first medal was claimed by the men's 3x3 basketball team just before 17:00 BST.

A couple of hours later, three more followed in the space of five minutes.

The women's wheelchair 3x3 basketball team took silver; Evans added her second gold - and third medal - of the Games in the 200m breaststroke; then Woods claimed gold in the women's T54 1500m.

Shaw then joined in with bronze in the women's S9 100m freestyle before MacInnes was edged into second place in the women's 200m butterfly to take her second individual silver of the meet.

Around the same time, MacKenzie was leaping to long jump bronze, before the haul was completed in the pool when Evans and MacInnes teamed up with Katie Shanahan and Evie Davis to take silver in the women's 4x100m medley.

Three more further medals are guaranteed in boxing - with fighters in semi-final action on Friday - while further prospects remain in athletics, bowls, cycling, judo and weightlifting.

fullText:
James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? 
It is difficult to believe that James Cameron’s Aliens was released into cinemas 40 years ago. The seminal space shooter took the original Alien – a tense slasher film with a tiny cast and one monster – and transformed it into an intergalactic war movie crammed with wry one-liners, massive guns and an actual boss battle finale. As a 14-year-old, I stood in line at the Tatton Gatley cinema, unsure if I’d be allowed in – I came out three hours later a changed person, my head filled with esoteric military slang and a deep fear of beeping motion detectors. For days afterwards, I slept with my duvet covering my mouth so that no facehuggers could get me. (I was a highly impressionable teenager.)

It’s little wonder that the film has had such a profound effect on video game design. Take the colonial marines, for example. Although the concept of the space soldier had been around in sci-fi novels since the 1930s, most notably in the works of EE “Doc” Smith and Robert Heinlein (the Starship Troopers), Hicks, Hudson, Vasquez and co, were the perfect 80s rendition, combining the witty banter of contemporary buddy cop flicks with awesome weaponry and hi-tech gadgets. Their influence is easy to spot in Doom, where the nameless marine fights ceaseless waves of hellish monsters using a mix of futuristic rifles and good old shotguns. It’s there too in the Halo series, the Spartan soldiers sporting the same armour and mega weapons, cruising about in very similar highly militarised starships and fighting recognisable hive-mind space beasts. Gears of War, Killzone and Marathon all borrow from the same set of costumes and deadly accessories.

Also important to future game designers was the way in which James Cameron opened up the world of Alien after Ridley Scott’s original locked-room mystery of a movie. He beefed up the Weyland-Yutani Corporation, giving us the stencil for dozens of evil video game mega corps; he brought in an array of weapons from handguns to M41A pulse rifles and the M56 smart guns, introducing the idea of a scaled armoury to discover and master; and he employed a structure based around the repeated rhythm of tense exploration followed by explosive encounters that countless games would follow.

It’s weird, then, how difficult it has proven to directly translate the movie into games. While the original Alien spawned a cult 8bit translation and the brilliant Alien: Isolation, Cameron’s sequel is best known for the disastrously bugged Aliens: Colonial Marines, which led to a lawsuit for deceptive marketing. Elsewhere, third-person co-op blaster Aliens: Fireteam Elite drew mixed reviews but has at least birthed a forthcoming sequel, and the 2D Metroid-style game Aliens: Infestation has plenty of fans. My favourite, though, was one of the two official tie-ins from 1986. Aliens: the Computer Game from Electric Dreams Software was a thrilling proto-FPS, allowing you to control several of the movie’s characters as they stalked through an atmosphere processing plant getting attacked by xenomorphs and facehuggers. I’m not sure it’s ever been bettered.

Watching the movie again this week, it’s impossible not to notice all the little scenic and narrative touches that have since shaped how sci-fi action games function. Even the sentry gun, which was cut from the cinematic release and only turned up in the special edition home release, has become a staple special weapon, present in everything from Call of Duty to Helldivers. I wonder how many of today’s game creators were also stood in cinema lines in the summer of 1986, too young to be there, not quite ready to have their minds blown for ever?

Those of us with an interest in the fibre arts are always delighted to see them crop up in other media. Here, embroidered character art helps Scarlet Deer Inn to stand out in a crowded market. Once players are in, they’ll find the charming medieval village has some horrific secrets. Players guide mother-of-two Elise through danger-filled caverns on a quest to find her children and prevent them from meeting a gruesome end, a goal that gained additional meaning when the husband-and-wife developers had a baby of their own. Armed only with a torch, you must keep it lit or likely repeatedly succumb to the darkness. Jordan Erica Webber

Available on: PC

 Estimated playtime: four hours

In what is likely to become a familiar problem for the games industry, Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI marketing schedule is being infiltrated by AI-generated trailers purporting to show scenes from the forthcoming game. Examples include a surfing video and a woman enjoying champagne on a yacht. As Eurogamer points out, the videos are filling a vacuum left by Rockstar’s somewhat stingy approach to releasing in-game footage. The company does not seem to be impressed.

Rather embarrassingly for console manufacturers seeking to go digital only, network outages are back. On Friday, PlayStation Network went down for several hours, leaving players with no access to their games. And on Monday, it was the turn of Xbox, a major outage making it impossible to sign in to user accounts, launch games or download content. While the PlayStation situation has now been resolved, the Xbox network was still having issues at time of press. All hail our disc-less future!

When Valve announced its new Steam Machine PC, fans were intrigued by a custom front plate the company had attached to the machine, which appeared to be an e-ink screen displaying performance data from inside the computer, such as memory and CPU performance. Now, Valve has released all the files and details for what it calls The Inkterface, so owners can build one – and gaming site Aftermath has done just that. Very nerdy, but very cool.

And if you enjoyed reminiscing about Aliens, you might want to check out forthcoming book Aliens: The Video Games by Mike Diver, a complete history of adaptations, including lots of developer interviews.

This week’s question is from Ben via email:

“I want to learn more about the history of video games and I wondered if there are any canonical lists of the best titles – perhaps a gaming equivalent of the BFI’s 250 Greatest Films of All Time or the American Film Institute’s 100 Years 100 Movies?”

Many publications that write about video games have their own top 100 list, although these tends to be compiled by their own critics or readers rather than a broader spread of experts. GQ, GameRant and Rolling Stone all have versions, while IGN has a “mathematically derived” list of the top 500, and we’ve done the best games of the 21st century (so far). For more formal attempts at developing a canon, the Strong Museum has a World Video Game Hall of Fame, MoMA has a games collection (but for some reason its website does NOT want you to find a definitive list!), and for its Art of Games exhibition in 2012, the Smithsonian compiled a list of 80 important titles with the help of gamers and game makers. There have also been a few books on the subject: try Penguin’s 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die (full disclosure: I wrote some of this book), BFI’s 100 Video Games, or Game On!: From Pong to Oblivion – The Greatest Video Games of All Time, compiled by ex-Edge magazine writers.

fullText:
SEATTLE (AP) — The 15-year-old arrested after a shootout at a food festival near Seattle's Space Needle over the weekend was armed with a ghost gun with an extended magazine, police said Tuesday.

Police Chief Shon Barnes told a news conference that the weapon was a 9 mm gun from Polymer80 — a now-defunct company that was once a leading manufacturer of ghost gun parts.

Investigators also recovered two other weapons and 14 shell casings that had been fired by weapons of two different calibers, he said.

The shooting in the waning hours of the three-day Bite of Seattle festival left three people dead, including a 19-year-old gunman, and at least four people injured, including a toddler. Authorities say they believe the violence was gang-related, and they are reviewing any available surveillance video and interviewing victims and witnesses in an effort to identify others who may have been involved.

An eighth person with a possible gunshot wound checked themself into a Seattle hospital after the shooting, but checked out before investigators could conduct an interview, Barnes said. Legal obstacles have prevented detectives from obtaining the patient's identity, he added. It's unclear if the injury was related to the festival shooting or whether the person might have been involved in it, but Barnes asked for the person to come forward and speak with investigators.

Ghost guns are privately made — often homemade — firearms that lack serial numbers used to trace them. They have often been purchased without a background check. Law enforcement officials say ghost guns, including those made with 3D printers, have been used in violent crimes across the U.S.

Lawsuits and state-level bans eventually pushed Polymer80 out of business in 2024, and last year, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a rule adopted under former President Joe Biden requiring companies to treat gun kits like other firearms by adding serial numbers, running background checks, and verifying that buyers are 21 or older.

The weapon the 15-year-old had been shooting when he surrendered to police was equipped with an extended 33-round magazine, Barnes said. The magazine still had 19 rounds in it.

At the scene Sunday night, police also recovered a 9 mm handgun that they do not believe was used in the shooting.

And on Monday, as food vendors were allowed to return to the area to clean up and collect their equipment, a third weapon was discovered: a Glock 45 model 9 mm with a switch allowing it to fire fully automatically, Barnes said. Police believe that gun was fired during the shooting. It had an extended 40-round magazine, with 21 rounds remaining in it.

In a document filed in juvenile court in Seattle on Monday, police said they believed there were at least three shooters: the 15-year-old, an acquaintance who died at the scene and "at least one other unknown suspect." Authorities had earlier said they believed there were two.

A judge on Monday ordered the 15-year-old to be held in juvenile detention for investigation of assault and firearms charges pending further hearings. The King County prosecutor's office said it expected to receive the case from police on Wednesday for a charging decision. Hong Tran, a public defender assigned to the teen's case, declined to comment in an email to The Associated Press on Tuesday.

The King County Medical Examiner's Office on Monday identified the dead as Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44; Ashley Whitehead, 56; and Junior Cee Niko Semo, 19.

Villalba was a husband and father of three known for his kindness and willingness to help others, according to a GoFundMe campaign launched Monday to help his family with funeral expenses. He died from a gunshot wound to his torso, while Whitehead died from a gunshot to her pelvis and Semo died from multiple gunshot wounds, according to the medical examiner's office.

Whitehead had just moved to Washington from Alabama a year ago and was enjoying the festival with one of her adult daughters when she was shot, her cousin Michelle Whitehead told The Associated Press. She was taken to the hospital and died in surgery, she said.

Ashley Whitehead adored her two adult daughters, and also loved nature and arts and crafts, her cousin said.

"I would consider her just a free spirit. She had the best sense of humor, the best gorgeous smile," she said.

During a vigil Monday night at the center, Michelle Whitehead stood among dozens of others with a sign that said "Whitehead Strong" as the group held a moment of silence and raised up flashlights on their phones to honor those that had been killed. Candles and flowers were arranged around them.

The four wounded included a 2-year-old boy, two men, ages 23 and 27, and a woman, 39, all of whom were discharged, a hospital spokesperson said.

One of the victims was walking a bicycle when struck, the court document said. The toddler was with his mother.

Rush reported from Portland, Oregon. Associated Press writer Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed.

fullText:
The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces

It starts on 4chan, in a May 2019 thread entitled “unsettling images”. The first post was a photo showing an empty room with the now iconic yellow wallpaper, no natural lighting and a kind of inexplicable jutting half-wall. Shortly afterwards, another user (there are no usernames on 4chan, just identifying numbers) responded with 78 words of text that would essentially lay out the blueprint for a future $262m A24 movie sensation.

“If you’re not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in the Backrooms,” the post begins. For the uninitiated, “noclip” refers to a game mode in which collision with solid objects is disabled, allowing players to move freely through walls and floors. Think of Chiwetel Ejiofor’s character in the film, finding a permeable wall in the basement of his furniture store and passing through to the world on the other side.

In games, noclip is intended for use by developers testing out their creations – but for decades now, players have been finding ways to access it themselves and reach hidden places they were never intended to see. It’s a phenomenon that Studio Chyr creative director William Chyr is intimately familiar with, both as a maker of games and as a player.

“Going behind the scenes, noclipping, and seeing the logic of the space, it’s like this Wizard of Oz moment of pulling open the curtain,” Chyr says. He remembers an early encounter with this in Batman: Arkham City: “There was this glitch that allowed you, if you kept spamming one of the grenades, to keep going higher and higher.” From there, the caped crusader could soar outside the level, into sections of Gotham that were only ever intended as a backdrop. “The streets had these cars that moved, but it was just a flat texture.”

Watching Backrooms, Chyr was also reminded of a similar bug in the notoriously janky Skyrim, where holding a wooden plate provided a quick way of noclipping out of the world. Looking at it from the outside in, players discovered that many of the game’s “tables” were in fact just bookcases embedded deep in the ground – just like the memorable Backrooms shot of a room in which the furniture is clipping through the floor. All these things that, in video games, the player is never meant to see.

The feel of Kane Parsons’ film is actually closer to these experiences than any of the many “official” Backrooms games that have popped up. The open-source nature of this mythos (as well as 4chan and Reddit, there are sprawling fan wikis cataloguing and expanding the lore) means that it’s possible to release your own game set in the Backrooms, using the name and iconography, in a way you couldn’t with another horror movie.

The most high-profile of these games, Escape the Backrooms, was first available in early-access form in August 2022, just months after Parsons’ first video. It offers a perfectly faithful recreation of the Backrooms aesthetic, from the yellow hallways to the yellow hazmat suits worn by agents of Async, the mysterious organisation only introduced towards the end of the film but a mainstay of the online incarnations. But all this is just wallpaper applied over the blueprint of a multiplayer survival horror game.

At its best, Backrooms taps into a sense of a place being “off”, in a way that’s unsettling but hard to pin down. It’s a delicate sensation, easily shattered (as it is in the film, I’d argue) by the presence of killer monsters. Even more so by the sight of another player in their gas mask and reindeer onesie, bunny-hopping through the hallways ahead.

Thankfully, there’s another stripe of Backrooms-inspired games offering nothing more than a self-guided tour through environments with a growing sense of weirdness and the constant suggestion of a threat lurking out of view.

Pools and Dreamcore both shine a spotlight on Poolrooms, an infinite swimming-baths dimension first glimpsed in one of Parsons’s videos and codified by the fandom as Level 37 of the Backrooms, with a similarly alien approach to architecture. In Dreamcore, it’s just one of a selection pack of realms to explore. You’ll also explore a “dead mall” and the looping corridors of a hotel: both abandoned and seemingly endless, like the spaces explored in the film, but with less of an obvious supernatural edge.

These malls and hotels are prime examples of a larger online taste for liminal spaces from which Backrooms is just one offshoot.

“These spaces always feel like they’re past their prime,” says Chyr. “It’s clear there was human activity here, at one point, but no longer.” His 2025 game Hotel Infinity is steeped in all these ideas, to the extent that at one point Hotel Liminal was considered as a title, Chyr says. “But I thought that was just too on the nose!”

Set in the lifeless corridors of a hotel seemingly designed by MC Escher, it’s a VR game that uses some clever spatial trickery to fold its endless halls into a 2x2m square of your living-room floor. One particular sequence late in Backrooms made me think of Chyr’s game – he confirms that he thought the same thing. “I was like, damn, I wish we’d done that!” he laughs.

Hotel Infinity is primarily focused on the impossible architecture of these places, something it shares with Exit 8 (also adapted into a film this year), a Japanese-made game that traps you in an infinitely looping section of a Tokyo metro station. The other side of the liminal coin is the sensation summoned by that original 4chan image: the eeriness of an empty place that no longer has any obvious function, or perhaps never did.

One game exploring this aspect is Interior Worlds, a “liminal photography” game in which you explore such spaces armed only with an SLR camera. The game’s developer, who goes by the moniker Sodaraptor, remembers first encountering the concept of liminal spaces “back in 2020, when the original Backrooms post on 4chan started going viral.”

It was an emotion they’d felt in such places but never previously had a name for. “A strange liminal discomfort”, Sodaraptor says, mixed with pangs of “anemoia”: nostalgia for an era that predates your own experience.

So it’s only fitting that the phenomenon’s virtual inspirations are now, in video game terms, as ancient as all those dead malls.

The aforementioned Arkham City and Skyrim both came out in 2011. The same year, Valve released Portal 2, the mind-bending first-person puzzler which Parsons has repeatedly cited as his biggest influence. The director even made a couple of Portal fan-videos; the last one was uploaded to his YouTube channel in 2021, just months before the first Backrooms clip.

It is probably inevitable that the aesthetics of these 15-year-old games would just now be beginning to seep through into the cinematic mainstream. Parsons was a young child when Portal 2 came out, and it’s only natural that he – and the generation of film-makers just now coming of age – would make things informed by the dark rooms they got lost in as kids.

A Minecraft Movie may already exist (unfortunately) but what will be much more interesting are the films and other artworks shaped by the experience of playing Minecraft at a formative age. Those dark caverns, the endless mines, the sounds of the zombies, the threat of the creepers – once those strange experiences have sunk into internet lore, who knows what will emerge and where it will take us.

title: SpaceX launches Starship on another test flight, this time with the most advanced Starlinks
description: NASA monitored the space-skimming flight, a critical step toward using the Starship as a lunar lander for moon crews.  The hourlong journey ended with a splashdown so soft that the spacecraft remained...
fullText:
SpaceX's mammoth Starship rocket blasted off Friday on another test flight stretching halfway around the world, this time releasing 20 of the most advanced Starlinks.

Towering 407 feet (124 meters), Starship soared from the company's base at the southern tip of Texas. NASA monitored the space-skimming flight, a critical step toward using the Starship as a lunar lander for moon crews.

The hourlong journey ended with a splashdown so soft that the spacecraft remained afloat in the Indian Ocean as the SpaceX webcast drew to a close, drawing cheers from employees back at the launch site.

Elon Musk's SpaceX had replaced six of the 33 engines on the first-stage booster after some of them failed to ignite last week, resulting in a last-second launch abort. The previous Starship flight in May also experienced engine trouble, which prevented the booster from making a controlled return.

This time, all of the engines fired at liftoff, but not enough of them lit back up for the booster's return, causing it to descend too fast and slam into the Gulf of Mexico. The spacecraft continued soaring eastward, popping out the Starlinks one by one 124 miles (200 kilometers) up before reentering.

It was the 13th flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, and the second this year of the new version dubbed V3. Like the previous demo, neither the booster nor spacecraft was meant to be saved, instead plunging into the sea.

The stainless steel, retro-looking spacecraft hovered upright over the Indian Ocean before lowering into the water, more than 10,000 miles (16,000 kilometers) from where the flight began.

It was the best reentry yet, according to SpaceX, with the intact booster floating amid just a few flames. Previous flights ended with the spacecraft engulfed in flames and exploding at splashdown — or rupturing in midair.

"We're really pumped about this," said SpaceX engineer Kate Tice, calling it "lucky flight 13."

The Starlinks accomplished all their jobs before reentering over the Indian Ocean.

After being ejected from the Starship's Pez-like dispenser, the Starlinks had just 20 minutes to communicate via lasers and radio before reentering. SpaceX said its engineers made contact and even downloaded data from each one. With more than 10,000 Starlinks currently providing internet, SpaceX boasts the world's largest satellite constellation.

Six of the newly launched Starlinks carried cameras that photographed Starship's heat shield at flight's end, beaming back amazingly crisp shots even as the spacecraft bobbed in the ocean. The heat shield was also equipped with sensors to measure the extreme pressure placed on the spacecraft during launch. Most of the heat shield's thermal tiles were black, but some were deliberately painted white to simulate missing tiles, part of an experiment to test the shield's robustness.

"We got all the heat shield data we needed and then some!" Musk said on X.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman offered congratulations. "Excited for what will be learned from this mission," Isaacman noted on X.

SpaceX wants to make sure Starship's heat shield can withstand the heat of entry before trying to return it to the Starbase launch pad near the Texas-Mexico border. The company already has used a pair of giant mechanical arms at the pad to capture a Starship booster. The company plans to do the same with the actual spacecraft, which is designed to be totally reusable.

NASA needs Starship to wrap up testing and reach orbit soon so the Artemis III astronauts — three Americans and one Italian — can practice docking their capsule with it next year.

Starship is also the vehicle with which Musk intends to build a city on Mars. He's already booking tourist trips to Mars, as well as the moon.

The latest test flight was delayed first by the July 16 launch abort, then again on Thursday by thick clouds from Tropical Storm Bertha.

title: I’ve been gaming for 40 years. Here are the best chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play
description:
Whether you’re on PC or a console, level up your setup with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs
